passage: For two days Marek and Santiago had been trading short, cold messages about a missed football practice. At 9 p.m., sitting on his bed in Warsaw with the heater ticking, Marek typed and deleted three angry replies. Then he wrote: 'Can I call you? I think we misunderstood each other.' The reply came fast: 'ok.' The phone rang. For a second neither spoke. Then Santiago said, 'So when you wrote "fine, whatever"...' and Marek groaned. 'I meant, like, oh well! Not I hate you!' 'It read like you hated me!' 'And you wrote "I have a life too"!' 'Because I thought you hated me!' There was a pause, then both burst out laughing. Five minutes in, two days of hurt felt ridiculous.

qa.q: How many angry replies did Marek type and delete?
qa.a: He typed and deleted three angry replies.

qa.q: What does the burst of laughter show about how both felt once they heard each other?
qa.a: It shows relief; hearing each other's voices made the hurt feel silly, as each realised the other had never meant to attack.

qa.q: Why was Marek's message a good turning point?
qa.a: Instead of another cold text, he suggested a call and named the likely misunderstanding, which invited Santiago in without blame.

qa.q: What might Santiago have felt when the phone rang?
qa.a: Probably nervous and a bit defensive at first, then relieved once Santiago could hear Marek's real tone 😊.

grounding: One teen asks to call because they misunderstood each other, and hearing each other's voices dissolves the hurt into laughter within minutes.

passage: Lights-out was at ten in the Dehradun boarding school, but the girls' hostel still glowed with phone screens. Hansa lay in the east wing staring at the chat with Arohi, in the west wing: a whole day of 'ok.', 'sure.', and one 'whatever you want.' She'd shown it to her roommate, who'd said Arohi was being fake. Hansa's stomach hurt. Finally she typed, 'Can I call you? I think we misunderstood each other.' Arohi replied, 'yes pls.' They whispered under their blankets. 'I thought you were angry about the dance partner thing,' Arohi said. 'I thought YOU were!' Hansa said. Hearing Arohi's voice crack, then giggle, Hansa felt half the knot in her stomach loosen within a minute. By the end they were both laughing into their pillows.

qa.q: Which wing was Arohi in?
qa.a: Arohi was in the west wing.

qa.q: What did Hansa feel once she heard Arohi's voice crack and then giggle?
qa.a: She felt relief as half the knot in her stomach loosened, realising they had both been misreading each other.

qa.q: Why did moving from text to a call work so quickly?
qa.a: Voices carry tone that short texts hide, so each could hear that the other was worried, not angry, and the hurt dissolved.

qa.q: How might Arohi have felt receiving Hansa's 'Can I call you?'
qa.a: Probably relieved and eager, since her quick 'yes pls' suggests she wanted to fix things too.

grounding: In a boarding hostel one girl asks to call her friend about a misunderstanding, and hearing each other's voices melts the hurt into laughter.

passage:
Dear Thatha,
You always say, "Talk, don't type." I finally did it.
Kamal and I hadn't spoken for three days because of a text fight about the football match. Everyone at school was taking sides. Last night I wrote, "Can I call you? I think we misunderstood each other."
He called. At first it was awkward. Then he said, "When you wrote 'nice going', I thought you were mocking me." I said, "I meant nice going! You scored!" There was a pause, and then we both started laughing. Five minutes, Thatha. Three days of sulking, gone in five minutes.
You were right. I'll tell you properly on Sunday.
Karthik

qa.q: How many days had Karthik and Kamal not spoken?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What was Karthik probably feeling when the call started?
qa.a: Karthik was probably nervous and awkward, unsure how Kamal would sound after the fight.

qa.q: Why did switching to a call work so quickly?
qa.a: Hearing each other's voices showed the real tone, so "nice going" was understood as praise and the hurt melted into laughter.

qa.q: What might Kamal have felt when he learnt "nice going" was praise?
qa.a: Kamal likely felt relieved and a bit silly, realising he had read mockery that wasn't there.

grounding: Shows a teen asking to call a friend after a text fight, and hearing each other's tone dissolving the hurt into laughter.

passage:
So, you know how Anand and I weren't talking? It was over one message. I'd written "sure, do what you want" about his party plan, and he took it as sarcasm. He replied something cold. Then the whole class got involved.
On Saturday I just thought, enough. I texted, "Can I call you? I think we misunderstood each other." My heart was going like crazy.
He called in two minutes. His voice sounded so normal. I said, "I wasn't being sarcastic. I really meant do what you want, it sounded fun." And he went, "Wait. Seriously?" And then he laughed, that silly honk laugh of his, and I laughed too. That's it. I'm Urmila, and I now call before I sulk.

qa.q: What had Urmila written about Anand's party plan?
qa.a: "Sure, do what you want."

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when she texted to ask for a call?
qa.a: Urmila was nervous, heart going like crazy, but determined to end the misunderstanding.

qa.q: Which choice turned this around, and why?
qa.a: Asking to call instead of texting more, because hearing Urmila's voice showed Anand there was no sarcasm.

qa.q: What is it like for Anand to hear Urmila's real meaning?
qa.a: Anand seems surprised and relieved, and his laugh shows the hurt dissolving.

grounding: Shows a teen asking to call after a text misunderstanding, and hearing each other's voices bringing relief and laughter.

passage:
My older sister Jahnavi had been stomping round the flat for two days. Something about Sunaina and a group chat. I heard her tell Mummy, "She called me dramatic, in front of everyone."
On Sunday evening, I saw her sitting on the balcony, typing slowly. Then she said out loud, maybe to herself, "Okay. Here goes." She showed me the screen before sending: "Can I call you? I think we misunderstood each other."
Ten minutes later, I could hear them. First quiet voices. Then Jahnavi said, "No, I thought you meant..." Then a pause. Then she laughed. A real laugh.
When she came in, she ruffled my hair. I don't know what they said exactly. But she ate two helpings at dinner.

qa.q: Where was Jahnavi sitting when she typed the message?
qa.a: On the balcony.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have been feeling when she said "Okay. Here goes"?
qa.a: She was likely nervous but brave, deciding to risk a call rather than keep sulking.

qa.q: Why did moving to a call help so much?
qa.a: Hearing Sunaina's voice cleared up what each had meant, so the hurt eased and laughter followed.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt getting Jahnavi's message?
qa.a: Sunaina may have felt relieved and grateful that Jahnavi reached out instead of letting the fight grow.

grounding: Shows a sibling watching a teen ask a friend to call after a text misunderstanding, with the call bringing laughter.

passage:
Thursday. For two days the chat between Anirban and Jahnavi had been nothing but short lines and full stops. "ok." "sure." "if you say so." Each message made the next one colder. Anirban lay awake that night, replaying them.
Saturday. After tuition he stood at the bus stop, thumb hovering. Then he typed, "Can I call you? I think we got each other wrong." She answered in a minute: "ok call." Her voice came through a little shaky. "I thought you were angry about the science model." "I thought YOU were angry!" Within five minutes they were laughing so hard that a man at the bus stop turned around to look.
Monday. They walked into the lab together. Jahnavi pointed at the half-built model and said, "Next time, call first."

qa.q: Where was Anirban when he typed his message?
qa.a: At the bus stop after tuition, on Saturday.

qa.q: Why did Anirban lie awake on Thursday night?
qa.a: He felt anxious and hurt, replaying the cold messages and unsure what had gone wrong.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking to call worked, because hearing each other's voices showed that neither of them was really angry.

qa.q: What was the call like for Jahnavi?
qa.a: She sounded shaky at first, worried he was angry, then relieved and laughing once she heard his tone.

grounding: Shows a teen moving a tense text exchange to a voice call, where hearing tone clears the hurt within minutes and laughter follows.
